extracted.intended_audience: readers, aspiring book reviewers, and writers interested in how The New York Times Book Review operates
extracted.subtask_description: Explains how The New York Times Book Review selects books to review and to include on year-end lists, how reviewers are chosen, and what makes a strong book review for their audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage rate (how many books are reviewed)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Book Review at The Times reviews about 1% of the books that come out in any given year."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates extremely selective coverage — most books will not be reviewed. This frames expectations about competition for attention and explains why many books are never covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Year-round winnowing for year-end lists
rubrics_metrics.description: "Basically, the entire year is a winnowing process that culminates in the 10 Best Books. We start thinking about it in January... Books come on and off that list of contenders, and in the course of the year, we check in on it periodically and update it... Toward the end of the year, around October, the process becomes more intense."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection for notable/year-end lists is continuous: editors set aside standouts as they encounter them, periodically reassess contenders, and intensify deliberation in the fall. The process is described as democratic through most of the year, with a decisive autocratic finish for final picks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pipeline: Editor's Choices → 100 Notable → 10 Best
rubrics_metrics.description: "Each week, we go through the previous issue and denote certain books as 'Editor's Choices'—these are the 9 books we especially like from that issue. At the end of the year, we pull together all of our Editor's Choices and narrow them down to 100 Notable Books of the Year—50 fiction and 50 nonfiction. From those, we pick the 10 Best."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being named an Editor's Choice is the first step toward year-end recognition; the formal funnel is weekly Editor's Choices, then an annual 100 Notable (split fiction/nonfiction), then the final 10 Best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection is primarily top-down
rubrics_metrics.description: "Here at the Book Review, the editors select which books we want reviewed, and then we find reviewers to write about them. We review all genres, though our tastes reflect the tastes of our editors and those of readers of The New York Times. The staff critics for The Times choose which books they want to review themselves."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors (not external callers/readers) determine which books get reviewed in the Book Review; staff critics at the broader Times may choose their own assignments. Taste and editorial judgment drive coverage decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection and assignment process
rubrics_metrics.description: "Each editor here handles a number of titles in a given week. They will come up with a list of possible reviewers and then bring it to my deputy and me. We then talk them over and sometimes add our own names to the list. Then we establish the order in which we approach people with the assignment... Sometimes, the first person on our list is too busy or has a conflict of interest... so we move to the next person on the list."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors compile reviewer shortlists, discuss assignments with senior editors, and approach potential reviewers in a prioritized order. Practical availability and conflicts of interest determine final assignment. Editors actively recruit 'smart new voices' from new authors, other publications, or direct pitch submissions with clips and specialty descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-of-interest rules for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sometimes, the first person on our list is too busy or has a conflict of interest (knows the author, shares an agent, blurbed an earlier book of theirs, etc.) and is disqualified, so we move to the next person on the list."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers who have personal or professional ties to the author (personal acquaintance, shared agent, previous blurbs, etc.) are disqualified from assignments to preserve impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre coverage shaped by editors' and readers' tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: "We review all genres, though our tastes reflect the tastes of our editors and those of readers of The New York Times."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although all genres are in scope, selection will be influenced by what editors and the publication's readership are interested in, which affects which books are chosen for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Best Books'—standards of selection
rubrics_metrics.description: "By 'Best Books,' we mean books that are extremely well executed in every sense: the scope of the work, originality of thought, writing on a sentence level, storytelling. It’s not necessarily about which books have the most 'important' message or a position we agree with. It’s about books we think will stand the test of time, and that people will want to read 5, 10, 20 years from now."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Year-end 'Best' selections prioritize ambition, excellence, execution across scope, originality, sentence-level craft, and storytelling — with an emphasis on durability rather than mere topical importance or ideological agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence between reviews and year-end lists
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is often the case that books we like don’t necessarily get hugely favorable notice in the Book Review... But we still named it one of the 10 Best Books of the year at the time. Our 10 Best is when we editors get to exert our own opinions, no matter what our reviewers say."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final year-end judgments are made by editors and can diverge from individual review verdicts; a negatively reviewed book can still be chosen as a Best Book if editors collectively value it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plot summary and spoilers (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think the biggest mistake reviewers make is conflating a book review with a book report. Generally speaking, readers don’t want to know what happens in a book, and they certainly don’t want (nor should they get) plot spoilers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reviews avoid excessive plot summary and do not spoil the book; they focus on engagement and assessment rather than recounting events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage intellectually and emotionally; provide depth and context
rubrics_metrics.description: "What I’m more interested in a review is seeing a writer engage with a book—intellectually and often, emotionally. I want some depth and context: What else has been written on the subject? What has this writer done previously? What kind of research did the writer do?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should offer informed engagement: situate the book within existing literature, consider the author's oeuvre and methods, and bring intellectual and emotional response to bear rather than only summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the book's writing through examples and description
rubrics_metrics.description: "I want to know what the writing is like—give me some examples, quote from the book, describe the style."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective reviews include illustrative quotations and concrete descriptions of voice, sentence-level craft, and stylistic features so readers can judge the writing itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer clear judgment: strengths, weaknesses, and reading-worthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: "I want to know what the writer does well and not so well. I want judgment. I want to know if a book is well done and if it’s worth my time. Is this a book I’ll actually want to read, or just read about?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should assess both positives and negatives, render a decisive evaluative stance, and tell readers whether the book is worth their time — a readable verdict is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial culture: collaborative, in-person discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: "At The New York Times Book Review, we have no staff critics—we are all editors and we sit together and we talk all the time... Having conversations around them—what books are you seeing, what looks good, what are you hearing, what do you like—are things we could talk about all day."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions are shaped by frequent, collaborative conversation among editors; editorial judgment is social and iterative rather than purely individual.
